outcome.answer:
A graph structure can reduce repetitive item lists by giving the generative reranker multiple valid transition paths instead of favoring a single high-likelihood sequence. In CONGRATS, the graph-structured model explores multiple paths, which expands the decoding space, promotes diversity, and explicitly models item dependencies through graph transitions; the paper presents this as a way to avoid the “likelihood trap,” where high-likelihood generative reranking outputs become repetitive [2].

Related papers suggest why this helps. Autoregressive generation can impose structural coupling so nearby items in the decoding tree receive similar probabilities, making them harder to distinguish; Latte mitigates this by creating multiple latent-token-conditioned trees, i.e., multiple paths through the decoding space [9]. TopoGR likewise preserves topology in the item ID space and uses topology-aware reranking to better capture item relatedness beyond exact token overlap [10]. These papers differ in the graph/structure used: CONGRATS uses an explicit graph-structured reranker for diversity [2], while Latte and TopoGR reshape or preserve the decoding topology to reduce structural bias in generation [9, 10].
